title: The Skull: Bones, Foramina & Fossae
summary: The bony architecture of the skull and every key opening that nerves and vessels pass through.

lessons.title: Bones of the Neurocranium: Frontal, Parietal, Temporal, Occipital, Sphenoid & Ethmoid

levels.kid:
Your brain is soft, a bit like jelly. So your body built it a strong helmet made of bone. That helmet is called the **neurocranium**.

It is made of eight bones that fit together like puzzle pieces:
- One **frontal** bone for your forehead
- Two **parietal** bones on the top and sides
- Two **temporal** bones near your ears
- One **occipital** bone at the back
- One **sphenoid** bone shaped like a butterfly, deep inside
- One **ethmoid** bone, small and spongy, behind your nose

The wiggly lines where the bones meet are called **sutures**. In babies, the bones are not joined yet. There are soft spots that let the head squeeze through at birth and let the brain grow bigger.
levels.hs:
The skull has two parts: the **facial skeleton** and the **neurocranium**, the bony case around the brain. The neurocranium has **eight bones**: four unpaired (frontal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid) and two pairs (parietal, temporal).

Its top is the **calvaria** (skullcap), and its floor is the **cranial base**.

- **Frontal**: forehead and the roofs of the eye sockets. It contains the frontal sinuses.
- **Parietal**: the large curved walls of the top and sides.
- **Temporal**: the sides and part of the base. It houses the hearing and balance organs inside its dense **petrous** part.
- **Occipital**: the back and base. It contains the **foramen magnum**, where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.
- **Sphenoid**: a butterfly-shaped keystone in the middle of the base that touches nearly every other cranial bone.
- **Ethmoid**: a light bone between the eye sockets that forms part of the nose and the floor under the frontal lobes.

Bones meet at **sutures**: the **coronal** (frontal-parietal), **sagittal** (between the parietals), **lambdoid** (parietal-occipital) and **squamous** (temporal-parietal). The **pterion** is an H-shaped area where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet. The skull is thin there, and the middle meningeal artery runs just underneath. That makes a blow to the side of the head potentially dangerous.
levels.college:
The neurocranium develops in two ways. The **calvaria** forms by **intramembranous ossification**: bone forms directly in mesenchyme. The **cranial base (chondrocranium)** forms by **endochondral ossification**, where cartilage is laid down first and later replaced by bone. Several bones are composite and contain both types.

**Bone by bone:**
- **Frontal**: has a squamous part (forehead) and orbital plates that roof the orbits. It also carries the supraorbital notch or foramen and the frontal sinuses. A persistent **metopic suture** between its two halves occurs in a minority of adults.
- **Parietal**: paired. The outer surface shows the parietal eminence and the superior and inferior temporal lines. Its inner surface is grooved by branches of the middle meningeal vessels and, along the midline, by the superior sagittal sinus.
- **Temporal**: has four parts. The **squamous** part bears the zygomatic process and the mandibular fossa. The **petromastoid** part holds the inner and middle ear, and the mastoid is pneumatized by air cells. The **tympanic** part surrounds the external acoustic meatus, and the **styloid process** projects downward from it.
- **Occipital**: has a squama with the external occipital protuberance (**inion**). Its lateral parts bear the occipital condyles, which articulate with the atlas. Its basilar part forms the **clivus** together with the sphenoid body.
- **Sphenoid**: has a body (containing the sphenoid sinus and the sella turcica), **lesser wings**, **greater wings** and **pterygoid processes**.
- **Ethmoid**: has a **cribriform plate**, a **crista galli** (anchor for the falx cerebri), a perpendicular plate (part of the nasal septum) and labyrinths that contain ethmoidal air cells. Their lateral walls form the paper-thin **lamina papyracea**.

**Craniometric landmarks**: bregma (where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet), lambda, pterion, asterion (parietal, temporal and occipital meet) and nasion.

**Fontanelles**: the anterior fontanelle closes at about 18-24 months; the posterior fontanelle closes at about 2-3 months.
levels.phd:
The neurocranium is a mosaic of tissues from different embryonic origins. Lineage tracing in mice using the Wnt1-Cre reporter (Jiang et al., 2002) showed that the **frontal bone is derived from neural crest**, while the **parietal bone is derived from paraxial mesoderm**. The **coronal suture** therefore marks a boundary between crest and mesoderm, and the two tissues are kept separate by Eph-ephrin signalling. The cranial base also has a dual origin: the prechordal part (ethmoid and anterior sphenoid) comes from neural crest, while the chordal part (basiocciput and the posterior part of the petrous temporal) comes from mesoderm. The boundary between them lies roughly at the sella and is set by the notochord.

Sutures are active growth sites, not just seams. Osteogenic fronts at the suture edges respond to FGF, TGF-beta, BMP and Wnt signalling, and the dura beneath them provides instructive signals. Two classic genetic examples show this:
- Gain-of-function mutations in **FGFR2** (Crouzon, Apert and Pfeiffer syndromes) and **FGFR3** (Muenke syndrome) cause premature suture fusion.
- Loss of **TWIST1** (Saethre-Chotzen syndrome) disrupts the boundary at the coronal suture.

Virchow's law (1851) describes what happens next: when a suture fuses early, skull growth stops perpendicular to that suture and continues parallel to it. Sagittal fusion, for example, produces scaphocephaly.

Composite ossification is typical of these bones. The **occipital** squama has a membranous part above the highest nuchal line and an endochondral part below it. Unfused remnants here, such as the **interparietal (Inca) bone**, can mimic fractures on imaging. The **sphenoid** ossifies from many centres; the greater wings are partly membranous. The **temporal** bone fuses from four components, and the **petrous** part is among the densest bone in the body. Ancient DNA researchers exploit this: they preferentially sample the otic capsule of the petrous bone because it preserves endogenous DNA unusually well.

Wormian bones are small extra bones within sutures, most often the lambdoid suture. They are common in healthy people. In large numbers, they are associated with osteogenesis imperfecta and cleidocranial dysplasia (caused by RUNX2 mutations). The **spheno-occipital synchondrosis** is a major growth plate for the cranial base and fuses in adolescence. Its timing is used in forensic age estimation.
levels.expert:
For a neurosurgeon, each neurocranial bone is a surgical approach and a source of potential hazards.

- **Pterion**: the pterional (Yasargil) craniotomy centres on it. Drilling the lesser sphenoid wing flat opens the Sylvian corridor to the circle of Willis. The middle meningeal artery often runs in a bony canal here, so a fracture at this point can tear it. That explains the textbook epidural haematoma with a **lucid interval**.
- **Frontal bone**: frontal sinus size varies greatly. If a bifrontal flap enters the sinus, the mucosa must be removed (exenterated) or the sinus sealed (cranialized). Otherwise there is a risk of a mucocele or of CSF leaking through the nose (rhinorrhoea).
- **Asterion**: used to locate the transverse-sigmoid junction for retrosigmoid approaches. However, its relationship to the sinus is variable. Many surgeons now place the keyhole using neuronavigation or the digastric groove instead of the asterion alone.
- **Petrous temporal**: anterior petrosectomy (Kawase) removes bone in the triangle bounded by the greater superficial petrosal nerve, the arcuate eminence and the trigeminal impression, without damaging the cochlea. Posterior petrosal approaches trade bone removal against the labyrinth. **Superior canal dehiscence** (Minor, 1998) is thinning of the bone over the superior semicircular canal. It causes sound- or pressure-induced vertigo and is repaired through a middle fossa approach.
- **Ethmoid**: the **lamina papyracea** and the **lateral lamella of the cribriform plate** are injury points in endoscopic sinus surgery. Keros classification of olfactory fossa depth predicts the risk of entering the skull base.
- **Bregma and the coronal suture**: Kocher's point, used for frontal ventricular drains, lies about 1 cm anterior to the coronal suture in the midpupillary line.

**Fracture patterns**: temporal bone fractures are now classified as otic-capsule-sparing versus otic-capsule-violating, rather than by the older longitudinal/transverse scheme. Violating fractures carry more risk of facial palsy, sensorineural hearing loss and CSF leak.

**Craniosynostosis repair** varies with age. Endoscopic strip craniectomy followed by helmet therapy is best before about 3-4 months. Spring-assisted and distraction techniques are other options, and open vault remodelling is used for older infants. One open question is whether early release improves neurocognitive outcome in isolated single-suture synostosis. The evidence is mixed.

Research frontiers include patient-specific 3D-printed cranioplasty implants (PEEK and titanium) and identifying suture stem cells (Gli1-positive and Axin2-positive populations) for biological strategies to regenerate sutures.

keyPoints: The neurocranium has 8 bones: frontal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid, plus paired parietal and temporal
Calvaria ossifies intramembranously; cranial base is mostly endochondral
Key sutures: coronal, sagittal, lambdoid, squamous
Pterion is thin bone over the middle meningeal artery
Sphenoid is the keystone; petrous temporal houses the inner ear
Frontal bone derives from neural crest, parietal from mesoderm

test.q: How many bones make up the neurocranium?
test.explain: Frontal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid, two parietal and two temporal bones make eight.

test.q: Which suture lies between the frontal and parietal bones?
test.explain: The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to both parietals; the sagittal suture joins the two parietals.

test.q: Why is a blow to the pterion clinically dangerous?
choices: The internal carotid artery runs along it
It is the thickest point and transmits force
The optic nerve exits the skull through it
Thin bone overlies the middle meningeal artery
test.explain: The pterion is thin, and the middle meningeal artery runs just beneath it, risking an epidural haematoma.

test.q: Which part of the temporal bone contains the inner ear?
test.explain: The dense petrous (petromastoid) part houses the inner and middle ear.

test.q: Which bone contains the foramen magnum?
test.explain: The foramen magnum lies in the occipital bone, where the brainstem continues as the spinal cord.

test.q: The calvaria forms mainly by which process?
test.explain: Skullcap bones form directly in mesenchyme. The cranial base is mostly endochondral.

test.q: The crista galli, which anchors the falx cerebri, belongs to the:
test.explain: The crista galli projects upward from the ethmoid bone, next to the cribriform plate.

test.q: The sella turcica sits on which part of the sphenoid?
test.explain: The sella turcica lies on the sphenoid body, above the sphenoid sinus.

test.q: Bregma is the meeting point of which sutures?
test.explain: Bregma is where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet; lambda is where the sagittal and lambdoid meet.

test.q: What is the name of the skullcap formed by the top of the neurocranium?
test.explain: The calvaria is the vault of the skull; the floor is the cranial base.

test.q: The paper-thin lateral wall of the ethmoid labyrinth is the lamina ___.
test.explain: The lamina papyracea separates the ethmoidal air cells from the orbit.

test.q: Small extra bones found within sutures are called ___ bones.
test.explain: Wormian (sutural) bones are common, especially in the lambdoid suture.

kidTest.q: What is the neurocranium?
choices: The bones that hold your teeth
The bony helmet around the brain
kidTest.explain: It is the bony case that protects the brain.

kidTest.q: Which bone is shaped like a butterfly?
kidTest.explain: The sphenoid looks like a butterfly and sits deep inside the skull.

kidTest.q: Which bone is at your forehead?
kidTest.explain: The frontal bone makes your forehead.

kidTest.q: Why do babies have soft spots?
choices: To help them hear sounds better
To keep their eyes in place
To let the head squeeze and grow
kidTest.explain: The soft spots help at birth and give the brain room to grow.

kidTest.q: The wiggly lines where skull bones meet are called s _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Sutures are the joints between skull bones.

advancedTest.q: Sagittal synostosis produces a long, narrow skull. Which principle explains this?
choices: Dural signals halt vault growth until the suture reopens
Growth increases at right angles to the fused suture to compensate
Endochondral cranial base growth overrides calvarial growth
Growth stops across the fused suture but continues along it
advancedTest.explain: Virchow's law: growth across a fused sagittal suture stops, so the skull lengthens front to back (scaphocephaly).

advancedTest.q: Why is the coronal suture a vulnerable site in TWIST1 and FGFR mutations?
choices: It lies directly over the superior sagittal sinus
It is the last suture to ossify in childhood
It develops by endochondral rather than membranous bone
It marks a neural crest-mesoderm boundary
advancedTest.explain: The frontal bone is neural crest and the parietal is mesoderm. The coronal suture marks this lineage boundary, which depends on Twist1 and Eph-ephrin signalling.

advancedTest.q: Ancient-DNA researchers prefer the otic capsule mainly because the petrous bone:
choices: Lies close to the brain and absorbs neural DNA
Is pneumatized, keeping its tissue dry
Is very dense and protects endogenous DNA
Ossifies last and therefore holds the youngest cells
advancedTest.explain: The petrous part is among the densest bone in the body, so it protects DNA better than most other skeletal sites.

advancedTest.q: A trauma patient has a temporal bone fracture with facial palsy and sensorineural hearing loss. Which classification best predicts this pattern?
choices: Squamous fracture with the capsule spared
advancedTest.explain: Fractures that violate the otic capsule carry more risk of facial palsy, sensorineural hearing loss and CSF leak.

lessons.title: Bones of the Facial Skeleton and the Mandible

levels.kid:
Your skull has two big parts. The top part is like a helmet that protects your brain. The front part is your face.

Your face is built from 14 bones. Most of them come in pairs, one on the left and one on the right, like a pair of shoes. Your cheekbones are called **zygomatic** bones. Your upper jaw is the **maxilla**. It holds your top teeth.

There is one face bone that can really move: the **mandible**, your lower jaw. It swings on little hinges just in front of your ears. Put your fingers there and open your mouth. Can you feel it move?

That is how you chew, talk and yawn. Every other face bone stays still, locked together like puzzle pieces.
levels.hs:
The skull is divided into the **neurocranium**, which surrounds the brain, and the **viscerocranium** (facial skeleton), which forms the face, holds the teeth, and frames the eyes, nose and mouth.

The facial skeleton has **14 bones**:
- Paired (2 each): **maxilla**, **zygomatic**, **nasal**, **lacrimal**, **palatine**, and **inferior nasal concha**
- Unpaired (1 each): **vomer** and **mandible**

The **maxillae** are the keystone of the midface. Each one holds the upper teeth, forms part of the orbit floor, the side of the nose, and most of the hard palate. Inside each sits a large air space, the **maxillary sinus**.

The **zygomatic bones** form the cheek prominences. They join the temporal bone to make the **zygomatic arch**, which you can feel in front of your ear.

The **mandible** is the largest and strongest facial bone, and the only skull bone that moves freely. It joins the temporal bone at the **temporomandibular joint (TMJ)**, a joint that lets the jaw both hinge and slide forward.

A real example: in boxing, a blow to the side of the jaw often breaks the mandible in two places at once, because the jaw is shaped like a ring with the skull. A break on one side commonly comes with a second break on the other side.
levels.college:
The **viscerocranium** develops largely from the first pharyngeal arch (maxillary and mandibular processes) and ossifies mostly by **intramembranous ossification**. Classical counts give 14 bones. Note that the ethmoid and sphenoid contribute to the face but are counted with the neurocranium.

**Maxilla.** It has a body containing the maxillary sinus, and four processes:
- **Frontal**: rises to meet the frontal bone at the medial orbit
- **Zygomatic**: articulates with the zygomatic bone
- **Alveolar**: holds the upper teeth
- **Palatine**: forms the anterior two-thirds of the hard palate

The **infraorbital foramen**, just below the orbital rim, transmits the infraorbital nerve (from V2) and vessels. The incisive canal opens behind the central incisors.

**Palatine bones.** Their horizontal plates form the posterior third of the hard palate. Their perpendicular plates line the nasal cavity wall. Each has a **greater palatine foramen**.

**Zygomatic bone.** It forms the lateral orbital wall and floor and the cheek. Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the arch.

**Small bones.**
- **Nasal** bones form the bridge of the nose.
- **Lacrimal** bones lie in the medial orbit and help form the fossa for the lacrimal sac.
- The **inferior nasal conchae** are separate scroll-like bones on the lateral nasal wall.
- The **vomer** forms the posteroinferior nasal septum with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid.

**Mandible.** It consists of a horseshoe body and two rami meeting at the **angle**. Each ramus ends in two projections:
- The **coronoid process**, where temporalis attaches
- The **condylar process**, whose head sits in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone

The **mandibular foramen**, on the medial ramus, admits the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), guarded by the **lingula**. The nerve exits as the mental nerve through the **mental foramen**, below the premolars. The **mylohyoid line** divides the inner surface into regions above and below the floor of the mouth.
levels.phd:
Developmentally, the facial skeleton is overwhelmingly **neural crest-derived**. Cranial neural crest cells migrate into the frontonasal prominence and first pharyngeal arch. In the arch, Hox-negative crest patterns the jaws. Dlx gene codes (Dlx5/6 in the lower jaw) set up the upper-versus-lower jaw identity, signalled by endothelin-1 acting through the EDNRA receptor. Knocking out Edn1 or Dlx5/6 in mice turns the mandible into a maxilla-like structure, a classic homeotic result.

**Meckel's cartilage** is the first-arch cartilage. It acts as a scaffold that the mandible forms beside, by intramembranous ossification; the mandible does not form by turning the cartilage into bone. Its dorsal end becomes the malleus and incus, and its sheath persists as the sphenomandibular ligament. The **condylar cartilage** is a secondary cartilage. It grows by adaptive endochondral activity, and it is a major growth site; injury in childhood can produce mandibular asymmetry or ankylosis.

The midface is a lightweight lattice of thin plates organized around thickened vertical and horizontal **buttresses** that carry chewing forces to the skull base:
- **Vertical**: nasomaxillary, zygomaticomaxillary and pterygomaxillary
- **Horizontal**: frontal bar, infraorbital rims and zygomatic arches, alveolar/palatal arch

This design explains how fractures behave. **René Le Fort** (1901) mapped three recurring fracture lines by dropping weights on cadaver skulls:
- **Le Fort I**: horizontal, through the maxilla above the teeth
- **Le Fort II**: pyramidal, across the nasal bridge and infraorbital rims
- **Le Fort III**: craniofacial disjunction through the zygomatic arches and the frontozygomatic and frontonasal sutures

All three cross the pterygoid plates.

The mandible behaves as a curved beam. Its biomechanically weak zones are the condylar neck, the angle (especially with an impacted third molar), and the parasymphysis near the mental foramen. With age and tooth loss, the alveolar bone resorbs. The mental foramen then comes to lie near the crest, and the gonial angle opens out. Bone tissue persists only where it carries load, a living example of Wolff's law.
levels.expert:
Clinically, facial bone anatomy is about airway, eyes, bite and brain.

**Imaging.** Thin-slice CT with 3D reconstruction is the standard of care; panoramic radiographs miss condylar and midline fractures. The "ring" principle matters: find one mandibular fracture, search for the second. A symphyseal blow classically breaks the condyles on both sides as well. Bilateral parasymphyseal fractures can let the tongue fall back and obstruct the airway.

**Neurosurgical overlap.**
- Le Fort II and III injuries often coexist with skull-base fractures, CSF rhinorrhea and carotid-cavernous injury.
- Blind nasogastric tube or nasotracheal intubation risks passage into the cranium through a disrupted cribriform region.
- Zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures disrupt the orbital floor and lateral wall. The results include enophthalmos, diplopia from inferior rectus entrapment (urgent in children: the "white-eyed" blowout with oculocardiac bradycardia), and infraorbital numbness.
- Craniofacial approaches exploit the facial skeleton as a corridor. Transmaxillary and transfacial routes to the clivus and skull base are classic examples, as are orbitozygomatic osteotomies, which remove the arch and rim to minimize brain retraction.

**Fixation.** Champy's lines of ideal osteosynthesis guide miniplate placement along the mandibular tension zones. Repair restores the buttresses first, because rebuilding facial height, width and projection depends on them. Bite (occlusion) is the reference: dental relationships are set before plating.

**Pharmacology tie-in.** Antiresorptive and antiangiogenic drugs, such as bisphosphonates, denosumab and bevacizumab, can cause **medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)**. MRONJ strongly favours the mandible, probably because of the jaw's high bone turnover, thin mucosa and frequent dental trauma.

**Frontiers.**
- Virtual surgical planning with patient-specific cutting guides and printed titanium plates is now routine for fibula-flap mandible reconstruction.
- Face transplantation has demonstrated composite bony allografts.
- Open questions include predicting condylar growth after pediatric fracture, the best approach for condylar fractures (open vs closed), and tissue-engineered bone that can match the mandible's load-bearing biology.

keyPoints: The facial skeleton (viscerocranium) has 14 bones; the mandible and vomer are unpaired
The maxillae are the midface keystone: teeth, palate, orbit floor, maxillary sinus
The mandible is the only freely movable skull bone, hinging and sliding at the TMJ
Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen and exits the mental foramen as the mental nerve
Facial bones are mostly neural crest-derived and form by intramembranous ossification
Midface buttresses explain Le Fort I, II and III fracture patterns

test.q: How many bones make up the facial skeleton in the classical count?
test.explain: The viscerocranium has 14 bones: six pairs plus the vomer and mandible. The figure 22 is the whole skull, and 8 is the neurocranium.

test.q: Which facial bone is unpaired?
test.explain: The vomer, which forms part of the nasal septum, is single; the mandible is the other unpaired facial bone.

test.q: Which bone contains the largest paranasal air space below the orbit?
test.explain: The maxillary sinus sits in the body of the maxilla.

test.q: The posterior third of the hard palate is formed by the:
choices: Horizontal plates of the palatine bones
test.explain: The maxillae form the front two-thirds of the hard palate, and the palatine bones form the back third.

test.q: The zygomatic arch is formed by the zygomatic bone joining the:
test.explain: The temporal process of the zygomatic bone meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone.

test.q: The temporalis muscle attaches to which part of the mandible?
test.explain: Temporalis inserts on the coronoid process. The condyle forms the TMJ instead.

test.q: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandible through the:
test.explain: It enters at the mandibular foramen on the medial ramus and leaves as the mental nerve through the mental foramen.

test.q: Why does a blow to one side of the jaw often cause two fractures?
choices: Teeth split the bone into halves
The mandible forms a ring with the skull
The TMJ dislocates on both sides
The jaw has a weak central suture
test.explain: The mandible and skull base act like a ring, so a break on one side often comes with a second break elsewhere.

test.q: The infraorbital nerve is a branch of which division of the trigeminal nerve?
test.explain: The infraorbital nerve continues from the maxillary division (V2).

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the jaw joint between the mandible and the temporal bone?
test.explain: The temporomandibular joint allows both hinging and forward gliding.

test.q: The upper teeth sit in the ___ process of the maxilla.
test.explain: The alveolar process carries the tooth sockets.

test.q: What scroll-shaped separate facial bone lies on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity?
test.explain: The inferior nasal concha is its own paired bone, unlike the middle and superior conchae, which belong to the ethmoid.

kidTest.q: Which face bone can really move?
kidTest.explain: The mandible (lower jaw) swings to let you chew and talk.

kidTest.q: What does the maxilla hold?
kidTest.explain: The maxilla is the upper jaw, and it holds the top teeth.

kidTest.q: Where are the jaw's hinges?
choices: At the back of your neck
kidTest.explain: The jaw joints sit just in front of your ears.

kidTest.q: What are cheekbones called?
kidTest.explain: Your cheekbones are the zygomatic bones.

kidTest.q: Most face bones come in pairs: for each bone on the left side of the face, there is a matching bone on the ____ side.
kidTest.explain: Paired facial bones such as the maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal and palatine bones have one on the left and one on the right. The mandible and vomer are single, unpaired bones.

advancedTest.q: Mice lacking Edn1 signalling develop a lower jaw resembling an upper jaw. This implies:
choices: Endothelin-1 is needed to form intramembranous bone
Lower-jaw identity is imposed on a default upper-jaw program
Hox genes pattern the first arch skeleton
Meckel's cartilage turns directly into the mandible
advancedTest.explain: Edn1-Dlx5/6 signalling gives the lower jaw its identity. Without it, the arch defaults to a maxilla-like fate. The first arch is Hox-negative, so the Hox option is wrong.

advancedTest.q: A child's condylar fracture worries surgeons more than an adult's mainly because:
choices: The mental nerve is easily torn
The condyle is a growth site
advancedTest.explain: Condylar secondary cartilage drives mandibular growth, so childhood injury risks asymmetry or ankylosis.

advancedTest.q: Why is blind nasal tube insertion hazardous in Le Fort II or III injuries?
choices: A tube may pass through the skull base
The maxillary sinus collapses onto the tube
The palatine bones press on the trachea
The vomer typically blocks the nasal passage
advancedTest.explain: These fractures often coexist with skull-base fractures. A tube can pass through the disrupted anterior skull base into the cranium.

advancedTest.q: Why does the mental foramen appear near the alveolar crest in an elderly person without teeth?
choices: The nerve migrates upward with age
advancedTest.explain: Without teeth to load it, the alveolar bone resorbs (Wolff's law), so the foramen ends up close to the crest.

lessons.title: Anterior Cranial Fossa: Cribriform Plate, Orbital Roofs & Openings

levels.kid:
Imagine the inside of your skull is like a house with three floors, stepping down from front to back. The top floor, right behind your forehead, is called the **anterior cranial fossa**. The front part of your brain rests there.

The floor of this front room is thin. Part of it is the roof over your eyes. In the middle is a tiny strip of bone full of little holes, like a salt shaker. It is called the **cribriform plate**. Tiny smell nerves drop through those holes into your nose. That is how smells reach your brain!

Because this bone is so thin, a hard bump to the face can crack it. Doctors watch for clear fluid dripping from the nose after an injury.
levels.hs:
The inside floor of the skull, called the **cranial base**, has three stepped levels called **fossae** (singular: fossa). The highest and most forward is the **anterior cranial fossa**. It holds the **frontal lobes** of the brain and the **olfactory bulbs**, which handle smell.

Three bones build this floor:
- The **frontal bone** forms most of it. Its **orbital plates** make the roofs of the eye sockets (orbits).
- The **ethmoid bone** sits in the middle. Its **cribriform plate** is a sieve-like strip with many tiny holes. Its **crista galli** is a small ridge sticking up like a rooster's comb.
- The **sphenoid bone** forms the back edge, through its **lesser wings**.

The tiny holes in the cribriform plate carry the **olfactory nerve fibers** (cranial nerve I) from the lining of the nose up to the olfactory bulb.

A real example: in a head injury, the thin cribriform plate can fracture. Then **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**, the clear fluid around the brain, can leak out of the nose. This is called **CSF rhinorrhea**. The person may also lose their sense of smell (**anosmia**) because the olfactory fibers are torn. Leaks like this matter because they open a path for germs to reach the brain and cause **meningitis**.
levels.college:
The **anterior cranial fossa (ACF)** is the shallowest of the three fossae. It supports the frontal lobes, gyrus rectus and olfactory tracts. Its posterior boundary is the **posterior free edges of the lesser wings of the sphenoid** laterally and the **anterior margin of the chiasmatic sulcus** (limbus sphenoidale) medially.

**Bony components**
- **Frontal bone**: its orbital plates form most of the floor and the orbital roofs. They are convex upward, ridged by gyral impressions (juga cerebralia), and often paper-thin.
- **Ethmoid**: the **cribriform plate** lies in a depression, the olfactory groove, between the orbital plates. The **crista galli** projects up in the midline and anchors the **falx cerebri**.
- **Sphenoid**: the body forms the **planum sphenoidale** (jugum), and the **lesser wings** end medially in the **anterior clinoid processes**.

**Openings and what passes**
- **Cribriform foramina**: olfactory nerve fila (CN I) running to the olfactory bulb, each wrapped in a meningeal sleeve.
- **Foramen cecum**: in front of the crista galli. It is usually blind in adults; in fetal life it can carry an emissary vein to the superior sagittal sinus.
- **Anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina**: on the frontoethmoidal suture, carrying the matching **ethmoidal arteries** (branches of the ophthalmic artery) and nerves (from the nasociliary nerve, V1) into the fossa and down into the nasal cavity. The anterior ethmoidal nerve runs briefly in the ACF beside the cribriform plate.
- **Optic canal**: in the lesser wing, at the back border. It carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery and is usually treated as part of the middle fossa region.

**Clinical correlations**
- Frontobasal fractures cause **CSF rhinorrhea**, anosmia, and periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes").
- **Olfactory groove meningiomas** grow from dura over the cribriform plate and can cause anosmia and personality change from frontal lobe compression.
- Inserting a nasogastric tube in a patient with a basal skull fracture risks entering the cranium. Oral routes are preferred.
levels.phd:
**Developmental and morphological detail.** The ethmoid ossifies from three centers: two lateral labyrinths, which ossify prenatally, and a median center for the perpendicular and cribriform plates, which ossifies during the first postnatal year. The cribriform plate joins the labyrinths around age two. The olfactory foramina form around fila that are already present, so the plate is effectively bone laid down around nerves. That is why it has so many perforations, often reported as around 40 or more per side, and why it is structurally weak.

**Depth and the Keros classification.** The cribriform plate sits below the level of the ethmoid roof (fovea ethmoidalis). The **lateral lamella** of the cribriform plate bridges the two, and it is the thinnest bone of the anterior skull base. **Keros (1962)** graded olfactory fossa depth:
- Type I: 1–3 mm
- Type II: 4–7 mm
- Type III: 8–16 mm

A deeper fossa means a taller, more exposed lateral lamella. Asymmetry between sides is common, and both features predict iatrogenic skull-base injury during ethmoid surgery.

**The anterior ethmoidal artery.** It leaves the orbit, crosses the ethmoid roof (sometimes hanging free on a mesentery below it), and enters the olfactory fossa through the lateral lamella. This point is the **weakest spot**, where CSF leaks most often occur. Laceration of the artery can retract it into the orbit and cause an orbital hematoma.

**Meningeal relationships.** Dura is tightly attached over the cribriform plate and crista galli. Arachnoid and pia continue along the olfactory fila as perineural sleeves. Experimental work in rodents and sheep, building on Bradbury and Cserr's studies, showed that CSF drains along these sleeves into nasal submucosal lymphatics. This cribriform route is now seen as a significant CSF outflow pathway alongside arachnoid granulations, although how much it contributes in adult humans is still debated.

**Fracture mechanics.** Frontobasal fractures spread along predictable lines through the thin orbital roofs and the cribriform region, sparing the stronger supports. The dura stuck to the cribriform plate tears together with the bone, which explains why a CSF fistula is so common at this site.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosing CSF leaks.** Beta-2 transferrin is the standard confirmatory test for CSF in nasal fluid. Beta-trace protein (prostaglandin D synthase) is a fast alternative but is less reliable in renal failure. The "halo" or glucose tests are outdated. For localization, use thin-cut CT to find the bony defect. Add CT or MR cisternography, or intrathecal fluorescein during endoscopy, when the defect is unclear. Most traumatic leaks stop within about a week with conservative care. Persistent leaks need repair because the lifetime risk of meningitis stays meaningful.

**Spontaneous leaks.** Many "idiopathic" cribriform and lateral lamella leaks occur in patients with **idiopathic intracranial hypertension** and obesity. These patients often have meningoencephaloceles and an empty sella. Repair without managing intracranial pressure carries higher recurrence rates.

**Surgical corridors.** Olfactory groove and planum meningiomas can be reached through these approaches:
- **Transcranial**: bifrontal, subfrontal, or pterional/supraorbital keyhole. These often preserve smell and give access to the lateral extensions.
- **Endoscopic endonasal transcribriform**: direct access to the tumor's base and its ethmoidal blood supply, but it sacrifices remaining olfaction and creates a large defect. This defect is usually closed with a **vascularized nasoseptal (Hadad–Bassagasteguy) flap**, which has greatly reduced postoperative leak rates.

Early devascularization means coagulating the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries. Hyperostosis of the planum or cribriform plate signals bony invasion that must be drilled out to lower recurrence (Simpson grade).

**Pitfalls.**
- Opening the frontal sinus during a craniotomy requires cranialization or exenteration of the mucosa to prevent mucocele and infection.
- **Tension pneumocephalus** after frontobasal repair or trauma (Mount Fuji sign on CT) can be a neurosurgical emergency.
- **Esthesioneuroblastoma** arises from olfactory epithelium at the cribriform plate. It is staged by Kadish and treated with craniofacial or endoscopic resection plus radiotherapy.

**Open questions.** How much the cribriform lymphatic route clears CSF and solutes in aging humans is unresolved. Reduced olfactory–lymphatic clearance has been proposed as a link between anosmia and neurodegeneration, but this remains a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism.

keyPoints: The anterior cranial fossa holds the frontal lobes and olfactory bulbs
It is built from the frontal orbital plates, ethmoid cribriform plate and lesser wings of the sphenoid
Cribriform foramina carry olfactory nerve fibers (CN I)
The crista galli anchors the falx cerebri
Anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina carry ethmoidal vessels and nerves
Frontobasal fractures cause CSF rhinorrhea, anosmia and meningitis risk

It may trigger a seizure directly

test.q: What is the medical term for loss of the sense of smell?

test.q: Bruising around both eyes after a skull base fracture is nicknamed ___ eyes.
test.explain: Periorbital ecchymosis, or raccoon eyes, suggests an anterior skull base fracture.

kidTest.q: What does the bone with tiny holes let through?
kidTest.explain: Tiny smell nerves go through the holes to reach the brain.

kidTest.q: Where is the anterior cranial fossa?
choices: At the back of your neck
kidTest.explain: It is the front, top floor inside the skull, behind the forehead.

kidTest.q: The holey bone looks a bit like a:
kidTest.explain: Its many small holes make it look like a salt shaker.

kidTest.q: After a face injury, doctors watch the nose for:
kidTest.explain: Clear fluid can mean the thin bone cracked and brain fluid is leaking.

advancedTest.q: A Keros type III olfactory fossa raises surgical risk mainly because:
choices: The crista galli becomes enlarged and pneumatized
The olfactory fila become fewer and thicker
The optic canal lies directly beneath the plate
A tall, thin lateral lamella is more exposed to injury
advancedTest.explain: A deeper fossa means a taller lateral lamella, which is the thinnest skull base bone and easily breached during ethmoid surgery.

advancedTest.q: A spontaneous cribriform CSF leak recurs after repair in an obese patient with an empty sella. The likeliest missed factor is:
advancedTest.explain: Raised ICP from IIH drives spontaneous leaks. Repairing the defect without managing pressure leads to recurrence.

advancedTest.q: Why is the cribriform plate so perforated and weak, according to its development?
choices: Bone forms around olfactory fila already present
Ossification starts there before the labyrinths
Venous sinuses erode it during adolescence
Air cells from the frontal sinus invade it
advancedTest.explain: The median ossification center lays bone around pre-existing olfactory fila, which leaves many foramina and a thin structure.

advancedTest.q: Choosing an endoscopic transcribriform approach over a transcranial one for an olfactory groove meningioma mainly trades:
choices: Better lateral reach for higher infection rates
Lower leak risk for loss of frontal lobe access
Shorter surgery for incomplete tumor removal
Early devascularization for loss of olfaction
advancedTest.explain: The endonasal route reaches the tumor's base and ethmoidal blood supply early, but it sacrifices remaining smell and leaves a defect needing a vascularized flap.

lessons.title: Middle Cranial Fossa: Sella, Superior Orbital Fissure, Rotundum, Ovale & Spinosum

levels.kid:
Inside your head, the skull has a floor with three steps, like a staircase going down from front to back. The middle step is shaped like a butterfly. Its two wings hold the sides of your brain, near your temples.

Right in the middle sits a tiny bony seat called the **sella**, which means saddle. A pea-sized gland called the pituitary sits in it. It is the body's boss gland and sends out hormone messages.

The floor has little holes, like doors in a wall. Nerves pass through them like wires, going to your eyes, cheeks and jaw. One small hole lets a blood vessel in to feed the skull's lining. Surgeons learn every door by name.
levels.hs:
The inside floor of the skull is divided into three levels called **cranial fossae** (fossa means a shallow pit). The **middle cranial fossa** is butterfly-shaped. Its narrow central body is part of the **sphenoid bone**, and its deep side wings hold the **temporal lobes** of the brain.

In the center is the **sella turcica** ("Turkish saddle"). Its deepest part, the **hypophyseal fossa**, holds the **pituitary gland**. Just in front of it the two optic nerves cross at the optic chiasm.

Key openings, from front to back:
- **Superior orbital fissure**: a slit into the orbit. It carries the nerves that move the eye (cranial nerves III, IV and VI) and the ophthalmic nerve (V1).
- **Foramen rotundum**: a round hole for the maxillary nerve (V2), which supplies feeling to the cheek and upper teeth.
- **Foramen ovale**: an oval hole for the mandibular nerve (V3), which supplies the lower jaw and the chewing muscles.
- **Foramen spinosum**: a small hole for the **middle meningeal artery**, which feeds the dura, the tough outer covering of the brain.

Real example: a blow to the side of the head at the **pterion** can tear the middle meningeal artery. Blood collects between skull and dura (an **epidural hematoma**) and needs emergency surgery.

A memory trick for the trigeminal branches: "**S**tanding **R**oom **O**nly", meaning Superior orbital fissure, Rotundum, Ovale for V1, V2, V3.
levels.college:
The middle cranial fossa lies at a lower level than the anterior fossa. Its front border is the lesser wings of the sphenoid, and medially it ends at the anterior clinoid processes and the chiasmatic sulcus. Its back border is the superior border of the petrous temporal bone, and medially it ends at the dorsum sellae. The floor is formed by the sphenoid body and greater wings, the squamous temporal bone and the anterior surface of the petrous temporal bone.

**Sella turcica.** Its parts are the tuberculum sellae in front, the hypophyseal fossa in the middle and the dorsum sellae behind, with the posterior clinoid processes on top. The diaphragma sellae, a fold of dura, roofs the fossa. The sphenoid sinus lies directly below, which is why pituitary tumors can be reached transsphenoidally. The cavernous sinuses lie on either side.

**Openings and contents:**
- **Optic canal** (lesser wing): CN II and the ophthalmic artery.
- **Superior orbital fissure** (between the greater and lesser wings): CN III, IV, VI, and the V1 branches (lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary), plus the superior ophthalmic vein and sympathetic fibers.
- **Foramen rotundum**: V2, which runs into the pterygopalatine fossa.
- **Foramen ovale**: V3, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein (sometimes an accessory meningeal artery). It opens into the infratemporal fossa.
- **Foramen spinosum**: the middle meningeal artery and vein, and the meningeal branch of V3 (nervus spinosus).
- **Foramen lacerum**: filled with cartilage in life. The internal carotid artery passes over it, not through it.
- **Hiatuses for the greater and lesser petrosal nerves** on the petrous surface, plus the **arcuate eminence** over the superior semicircular canal.

**Trigeminal impression**: a depression near the petrous apex that holds the trigeminal ganglion within **Meckel's cave**.

**Superior orbital fissure syndrome**: ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and V1 numbness. If the optic canal is also involved (vision loss), it becomes **orbital apex syndrome**.
levels.phd:
The middle fossa forms in two ways. The sphenoid body and lesser wings form by endochondral ossification within the chondrocranium. Parts of the greater wings and the temporal squama form by intramembranous ossification. Neurovascular foramina form as the bone ossifies around nerves and vessels that are already in place. This explains why foramen spinosum is the most variable of the openings. Its absence is reported in roughly 0.5 to 3 percent of sides, usually when the middle meningeal artery arises from the ophthalmic artery, a persistent anastomosis left over from the stapedial artery system.

Analysis of the **superior orbital fissure** depends on the **annulus of Zinn**, the common tendinous ring:
- **Outside the annulus (lateral, superior part)**: lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, trochlear nerve, superior ophthalmic vein. The mnemonic is "Live Frankly To See."
- **Within the annulus (oculomotor foramen)**: the superior and inferior divisions of CN III, the nasociliary nerve and the abducens nerve. Sympathetic fibers usually travel with nasociliary.
- The inferior ophthalmic vein often passes through or below the inferior part.

This arrangement explains why a lesion confined to the lateral fissure can spare CN III and VI.

**Foramen ovale morphometry.** In adults it averages about 7 mm long and 3 to 4 mm wide, and it is asymmetric in many skulls. Bony spurs or a partly ossified pterygospinous or pterygoalar ligament can narrow or hide its exterior opening. Martin Kirschner first used foramen ovale cannulation for trigeminal neuralgia in 1931. Today it is the basis of percutaneous rhizotomy (radiofrequency, glycerol or balloon compression) using Härtel's facial landmarks.

**Kawase's triangle** lies on the petrous apex. Its borders are the GSPN laterally, the trigeminal impression or V3 anteriorly, the arcuate eminence posteriorly and the petrous ridge medially. Drilling it opens a route to the posterior fossa without harming the cochlea, which lies just lateral to the meatal plane.

**Dehiscences** of the tegmen tympani or of the bone over the superior semicircular canal (Minor's syndrome, 1998) are thought to arise from developmental thinning plus age-related bone loss. Whether they are congenital or acquired is still debated.
levels.expert:
For the skull-base surgeon, the middle fossa matters most because of what it gives access to.

**Extradural middle fossa approach (House, 1961).** It is used for small intracanalicular vestibular schwannomas with useful hearing and for repair of superior canal dehiscence. After a temporal craniotomy centered roughly two-thirds in front of the external auditory canal, the dura is elevated from posterior to anterior. Elevating from posterior to anterior protects the GSPN, because the geniculate ganglion is dehiscent in a meaningful minority of people. Traction on the GSPN can pull on the geniculate ganglion and cause facial palsy. The middle meningeal artery is coagulated and cut at the foramen spinosum, which is the key landmark for the anterior limit of the dissection. Landmarks for finding the internal auditory canal include the Fisch method (the canal lies about 60 degrees from the arcuate eminence along the GSPN line) and the Garcia-Ibanez method, which bisects the GSPN–arcuate angle medially. The arcuate eminence may not sit exactly over the superior canal, so navigation is often added.

**Pitfalls:**
- Retractor injury to the temporal lobe or the vein of Labbé, which can cause venous infarction and aphasia on the dominant side.
- A CSF leak through opened tegmen air cells, which presents as otorrhea or rhinorrhea through the eustachian tube.
- Unexpected bleeding from the foramen ovale emissary veins or a sphenopetrosal sinus.

**Imaging.** Thin-slice CT shows the foramina directly. A widened or eroded foramen ovale or rotundum on MRI suggests perineural tumor spread, for example from adenoid cystic carcinoma or cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma traveling along V3 or V2. Loss of normal fat in the pterygopalatine fossa is an early sign. Denervation atrophy of the muscles of mastication points to V3 involvement.

**Spontaneous middle fossa CSF leaks and encephaloceles** are increasingly linked to idiopathic intracranial hypertension and obesity. Treating raised pressure after repair lowers the recurrence rate.

**Recent advances.** Endoscopic endonasal transpterygoid routes now reach Meckel's cave and the medial middle fossa, using the vidian canal and V2 as guides. This challenges the role of open lateral approaches. Head-to-head outcome comparisons are still open questions.

In trigeminal neuralgia, foramen ovale access now competes with microvascular decompression and radiosurgery. Choosing among them depends on age, whether the pain is typical and whether imaging shows a neurovascular conflict.

keyPoints: Middle fossa: butterfly-shaped, sphenoid body centrally, temporal lobes laterally
Sella turcica's hypophyseal fossa holds the pituitary, with the sphenoid sinus below
Superior orbital fissure carries CN III, IV, VI, V1 and the ophthalmic veins
Rotundum carries V2, ovale carries V3 ('Standing Room Only')
Spinosum carries the middle meningeal artery, the classic epidural hematoma source
Foramen spinosum, the GSPN and the arcuate eminence guide middle fossa surgery

test.explain: Rotundum carries V2 into the pterygopalatine fossa. V3 uses foramen ovale and V1 uses the superior orbital fissure.

test.explain: The optic nerve passes through the optic canal. The others all go through the superior orbital fissure.

test.explain: The hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica holds the pituitary. The trigeminal ganglion sits in Meckel's cave.

test.explain: The sphenoid sinus sits beneath the sella. The cavernous sinuses lie beside it, not below it.

test.explain: Arterial blood collects between the skull and the dura, which is an epidural hematoma.

test.q: Foramen ovale transmits V3 and also the:
test.explain: The lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein accompany V3. The greater petrosal nerve runs in its own hiatus.

test.q: What is true of the internal carotid artery at foramen lacerum?
choices: It branches into the meningeal arteries
It enters the orbit beside it
It passes over its upper surface
It exits the skull through it
test.explain: Lacerum is filled with cartilage in life, and the internal carotid artery passes over it, not through it.

test.q: Ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, V1 numbness and vision loss together suggest:
test.explain: Adding optic nerve involvement (vision loss) turns superior orbital fissure syndrome into orbital apex syndrome.

test.q: Name the saddle-shaped bony seat in the middle of the sphenoid that holds the pituitary.
test.explain: Sella turcica means 'Turkish saddle'.

test.q: The trigeminal ganglion lies in a dural pocket called ___ cave.
test.explain: Meckel's cave sits over the trigeminal impression near the petrous apex.

test.q: The mnemonic 'Standing Room Only' matches V1, V2 and V3 to the superior orbital fissure, rotundum and foramen ___.
test.explain: V3 exits through foramen ovale.

kidTest.q: What sits in the bony seat called the sella?
kidTest.explain: The pea-sized pituitary, the boss gland, sits there.

kidTest.q: What shape is the middle step of the skull floor?
kidTest.explain: It has a narrow middle and two wide wings, like a butterfly.

kidTest.q: What goes through the holes in the skull floor?
kidTest.explain: Nerves pass through like wires, and a blood vessel comes in through one small hole.

kidTest.q: The nerves passing through these holes go to which places?
kidTest.explain: These nerves serve the face, eyes and jaw.

kidTest.q: Sella means a horse rider's seat: s _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Sella means saddle.

advancedTest.q: A lesion in the lateral superior orbital fissure, outside the annulus of Zinn, would most likely spare:
advancedTest.explain: CN III and VI pass inside the annulus, while the lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein lie outside it.

advancedTest.q: Why is foramen spinosum sometimes absent?
choices: V3 takes over the meningeal blood supply
The dura receives its supply from the cavernous sinus
The middle meningeal artery arises from the ophthalmic artery
The foramen fuses with lacerum during ossification
advancedTest.explain: Foramina form around vessels already in place. If the middle meningeal artery comes from the ophthalmic artery, no spinosum is needed.

advancedTest.q: Why is the dura elevated from posterior to anterior in the middle fossa approach?
choices: To reach foramen rotundum before the cochlea
To avoid the internal carotid artery at lacerum
To protect the GSPN and a dehiscent geniculate ganglion
To spare the vein of Labbé at the petrous apex
advancedTest.explain: Elevating in this direction avoids pulling on the GSPN, which could tug the geniculate ganglion and cause facial palsy.

advancedTest.q: A patient with skin cancer develops wasting of the chewing muscles and a widened foramen ovale on MRI. This suggests:
choices: Spread along the middle meningeal artery
advancedTest.explain: V3 passes through ovale and supplies the muscles of mastication. V2 would widen rotundum instead.

lessons.title: Posterior Cranial Fossa: Foramen Magnum, Jugular Foramen & Hypoglossal Canal

levels.kid:
Your skull is like a house with three floors inside. The lowest, deepest floor is at the back. It is called the **posterior cranial fossa**. It holds the brainstem and the little brain, the **cerebellum**, which helps you balance.

This floor has holes, like doors, so important things can pass in and out.

- The biggest door is the **foramen magnum**, which means "great hole." The spinal cord goes through it to reach your body.
- Another door lets a big vein drain blood and lets nerves for swallowing and talking pass.
- A small tunnel carries the nerve that moves your tongue.

Brain surgeons know these doors very well, like knowing every door in their own house.
levels.hs:
The inside of the skull base has three stepped levels called **cranial fossae**. The **posterior cranial fossa** is the deepest and largest. It sits mostly in the **occipital bone**, with parts of the temporal bones and a small piece of the sphenoid bone. It holds the **brainstem** (pons and medulla) and the **cerebellum**. A tough sheet of dura called the **tentorium cerebelli** roofs it over.

Key openings, called **foramina** (singular: foramen):
- **Foramen magnum**: the largest opening in the skull. The medulla becomes the spinal cord here. The vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve also pass through it.
- **Jugular foramen**: a gap between the temporal and occipital bones. It carries cranial nerves **IX** (glossopharyngeal), **X** (vagus) and **XI** (accessory), plus blood that becomes the **internal jugular vein**.
- **Hypoglossal canal**: carries cranial nerve **XII**, which moves the tongue.
- **Internal acoustic meatus**: carries nerves VII and VIII toward the ear.

Real example: in a **Chiari I malformation**, the lowest parts of the cerebellum, the tonsils, sag down through the foramen magnum. This can press on the brainstem and block the flow of spinal fluid, causing headaches made worse by coughing. Surgeons may widen the opening to make more room.
levels.college:
The **posterior cranial fossa** is bounded in front by the dorsum sellae and the **clivus**, at the sides by the petrous ridges of the temporal bones, and behind by the occipital squama. The **tentorium cerebelli** forms its roof. The internal occipital protuberance marks the **confluence of sinuses**. From there, the **transverse sinus** grooves run laterally and turn down as the S-shaped **sigmoid sinus** grooves, which lead to the jugular foramen.

**Foramen magnum** (occipital bone), contents:
- Medulla/spinal cord junction and meninges
- Vertebral arteries, anterior and posterior spinal arteries
- Spinal roots of CN XI ascending into the skull
- Tectorial membrane and apical/alar ligaments at its anterior rim

**Jugular foramen** (between petrous temporal and occipital bones). It is classically divided into two parts:
- **Pars nervosa** (anteromedial): CN IX and the inferior petrosal sinus
- **Pars vascularis** (posterolateral): CN X, CN XI and the sigmoid sinus, which becomes the internal jugular vein at the **jugular bulb**

**Hypoglossal canal**: lies above the occipital condyle and carries CN XII and a meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery. It also carries a venous plexus.

**Internal acoustic meatus**: carries CN VII, CN VIII and the labyrinthine artery.

**Condylar (posterior condylar) canal**: an inconstant emissary vein channel.

Clinical correlations:
- **Vernet syndrome** (jugular foramen syndrome) means palsies of IX, X and XI. Signs include dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of the gag reflex and weakness of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid.
- **CN XII palsy** makes the tongue deviate *toward* the weak side when protruded.
- Raised pressure in the posterior fossa can cause **tonsillar herniation** through the foramen magnum. This compresses medullary respiratory centers.

The posterior fossa is small and tightly bounded, so even modest masses or swelling quickly cause hydrocephalus or brainstem compression.
levels.phd:
Developmentally, the occipital bone is a hybrid. The squama above the superior nuchal line forms in membrane. The basi-occiput, the exocciputs (condyles) and the lower squama form in cartilage from **occipital sclerotomes**, roughly four fused somites. This segmental origin explains anomalies at the foramen magnum: **proatlas** remnants, the **condylus tertius**, basilar invagination and atlanto-occipital assimilation. The **hypoglossal canal** is sometimes divided by a bony bridge, which echoes the segmental hypoglossal rootlets.

The jugular foramen is not a simple hole. Classic texts describe two compartments, split by the **intrajugular processes**, which may be joined by fibrous or bony septa. Rhoton's microsurgical work instead described three parts:
- A **petrosal** part, carrying the inferior petrosal sinus
- A **sigmoid** part, carrying the sigmoid sinus to the jugular bulb
- An **intrajugular (neural)** part, carrying IX, X and XI

These nerves pierce the dura through separate openings. CN IX enters through the glossopharyngeal meatus and is separated from X and XI by a dural septum. Its inferior ganglion lies in the **petrosal fossula**, the source of the tympanic (Jacobson's) nerve. The foramen is usually larger on the right, because the right sigmoid sinus is usually dominant.

Morphometrics of the foramen magnum are clinically relevant. In adults it measures about 35 mm long and 30 mm wide. Craniometric lines such as **Chamberlain's** and **McRae's** lines, and the clivus-canal angle, are used to define basilar invagination.

The nature of Chiari I malformation remains debated. Much evidence supports a **small, underdeveloped posterior fossa** due to occipital sclerotome underdevelopment (Nishikawa et al., 1997). Other cases are secondary, for example to intracranial hypotension or craniosynostosis. Tonsillar descent of more than 5 mm below McRae's line is a radiological convention, not a strict disease threshold. Many people with this finding have no symptoms, while some symptomatic patients have less descent. CSF flow dynamics at the foramen magnum, measured with phase-contrast MRI, may matter more than the amount of descent alone.

The **craniovertebral junction** (occiput, C1, C2) depends on ligaments for stability. The alar ligaments limit rotation, while the tectorial membrane continues the posterior longitudinal ligament up to the clivus.
levels.expert:
Operative access to the posterior fossa follows the bone.

**Suboccipital craniotomy and Chiari decompression.** Surgeons remove the posterior rim of the foramen magnum and often the arch of C1. Opinion is still divided on whether to open the dura and reconstruct it with a graft (duraplasty) or to split only its outer layer. Duraplasty probably lowers reoperation rates but brings more CSF-related complications. The pediatric Chiari–syrinx comparative effectiveness studies (Park Reeves Syringomyelia Research Consortium) have refined, but not settled, this question. A classic pitfall is missing **ventral compression**, for example from basilar invagination or a retroflexed odontoid. A posterior-only decompression can then fail and worsen instability; occipitocervical fixation or a transoral/endonasal odontoidectomy may be needed.

**Far-lateral (transcondylar) approach.** This approach reaches ventral foramen magnum meningiomas and vertebral artery aneurysms by drilling the posterior occipital condyle. The **hypoglossal canal** sets the limit of safe condylar removal. It lies roughly one-third of the way from the back of the condyle, angled anterolaterally. Removing more than about half of the condyle risks instability. The **V3 segment of the vertebral artery** in the suboccipital triangle, and the condylar emissary vein, are key landmarks and bleeding sources.

**Jugular foramen tumors.** The main types are **paragangliomas** (glomus jugulare), schwannomas of the lower cranial nerves, and meningiomas.
- Paragangliomas spread through the jugular bulb and erode the jugulocarotid spine. They are graded by the **Fisch** and Glasscock–Jackson systems and often need preoperative embolization.
- Schwannomas typically produce a smooth, dumbbell-shaped enlargement.
- Post-treatment palsies of IX and X are often more disabling than the tumor, causing aspiration and dysphonia. Many centers therefore favor subtotal resection plus **stereotactic radiosurgery**, or radiosurgery alone, to preserve function.

**Imaging pitfalls.** A **high-riding or dehiscent jugular bulb** and an asymmetric, normal right-dominant foramen are often mistaken for tumors. A **jugular foramen pseudolesion** caused by mixing of blood flow is another common mimic on MRI.

**Collet–Sicard syndrome** means palsies of IX–XII from a lesion near both the jugular foramen and the hypoglossal canal, such as occipital condyle fractures, carotid dissection or metastases. **Villaret syndrome** adds Horner syndrome, which points to the retrostyloid parapharyngeal space.

Open questions include patient selection in Chiari I, the place of endoscopic endonasal access to the lower clivus, and the long-term behavior of lower cranial nerve function after radiosurgery.

keyPoints: Posterior fossa: deepest fossa, mostly occipital bone, holds brainstem and cerebellum, roofed by tentorium
Foramen magnum: medulla-cord junction, vertebral arteries, spinal roots of CN XI
Jugular foramen: CN IX, X, XI and sigmoid sinus becoming the internal jugular vein
Hypoglossal canal carries CN XII; the tongue deviates toward the lesioned side
Chiari I: cerebellar tonsils descend through the foramen magnum
Jugular foramen syndromes: Vernet (IX-XI), Collet-Sicard (IX-XII), Villaret (adds Horner)

test.q: Which bone forms most of the posterior cranial fossa?
test.explain: The occipital bone forms most of the fossa, with help from the temporal bones and a small part of the sphenoid.

test.q: Which cranial nerves pass through the jugular foramen?
test.explain: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves exit there. XII uses the hypoglossal canal, and VII and VIII use the internal acoustic meatus.

test.q: The sigmoid sinus continues at the jugular foramen as the:
test.explain: The sigmoid sinus becomes the internal jugular vein at the jugular bulb.

test.q: Which structure passes through the foramen magnum?
test.explain: The vertebral arteries enter the skull through the foramen magnum. The internal carotid uses the carotid canal.

test.q: A patient's tongue deviates to the left when protruded. The likely lesion is the:
test.explain: The tongue deviates toward the weak side, because the healthy side's genioglossus pushes it over.

test.q: In Chiari I malformation, which structures descend through the foramen magnum?
test.explain: The cerebellar tonsils sag below the foramen magnum. Uncal herniation involves the temporal lobe and the tentorium instead.

test.q: Vernet syndrome combines palsies of which nerves?
test.explain: Vernet (jugular foramen) syndrome affects IX, X and XI, causing dysphagia, hoarseness and shoulder weakness.

test.q: The dural fold that roofs the posterior cranial fossa is the:
test.explain: The tentorium cerebelli separates the cerebellum from the occipital lobes above it.

test.q: Which structures pass through the internal acoustic meatus?
test.explain: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, with the labyrinthine artery, travel through the internal acoustic meatus.

test.q: Cranial nerve XII leaves the skull through the ___ canal.
test.explain: The hypoglossal canal lies above the occipital condyle.

test.q: What is the Latin name for the 'great hole' at the base of the skull?
test.explain: Foramen magnum is Latin for 'great hole', the largest opening in the skull.

test.q: The sloping bone in front of the brainstem, running from the dorsum sellae to the foramen magnum, is the ___.
test.explain: The clivus forms the anterior wall of the posterior fossa.

kidTest.q: What does 'foramen magnum' mean?
kidTest.explain: It means 'great hole', the biggest opening in the skull.

kidTest.q: What goes through the foramen magnum?
kidTest.explain: The spinal cord passes through it to reach the body.

kidTest.q: Which part of the brain helps with balance?
kidTest.explain: The cerebellum, the little brain, helps you balance.

kidTest.q: What does the nerve in the small tunnel move?
kidTest.explain: That nerve moves your tongue.

kidTest.q: The posterior fossa is the lowest ___ inside the skull house. (f _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: The skull has three inside floors, and the back one is the deepest.

advancedTest.q: A patient has dysphagia, hoarseness, trapezius weakness and tongue deviation, but no Horner syndrome. The best localization is:
choices: Internal acoustic meatus with spread into the cerebellopontine angle
Occipital condyle region near the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal
Isolated intrajugular part of the jugular foramen
Retrostyloid parapharyngeal space involving the sympathetic trunk
advancedTest.explain: Palsies of IX–XII without Horner syndrome are Collet–Sicard syndrome, as seen with condyle fractures. Adding Horner syndrome would point to the retrostyloid space (Villaret).

advancedTest.q: In a far-lateral transcondylar approach, why does the hypoglossal canal limit condylar drilling?
choices: It contains the main V3 vertebral artery segment along its whole length
It marks where the sigmoid sinus first enters the jugular bulb
It lies within the condyle, and deeper drilling risks CN XII and stability
It is the attachment site of the tectorial membrane onto the clivus
advancedTest.explain: The canal runs through the condyle. Drilling into it injures CN XII, and removing more than about half the condyle risks instability.

advancedTest.q: Why might posterior-only Chiari decompression fail in a patient with basilar invagination?
choices: The tonsils regrow above the rim of the foramen magnum
The jugular foramen narrows after bone is removed
Duraplasty itself creates a lasting ventral CSF block
Ventral compression by the odontoid is left untreated
advancedTest.explain: Basilar invagination compresses the brainstem from the front. Removing bone from behind does not relieve this and may worsen instability.

advancedTest.q: MRI shows the right jugular foramen larger than the left in a patient without lower cranial nerve deficits. The most likely explanation is:
choices: A schwannoma of the vagus nerve
advancedTest.explain: The right sigmoid sinus and jugular bulb are usually dominant, so asymmetry is a common normal variant that can mimic a tumor.
